prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single B027 prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The chair's summary shows that all six of us reached the same trio, and I note that the chair moved to it after hearing colleagues, so this is not six independent confirmations of one attribution. The scientific case still has to carry it, and it does. The incretin effect and proglucagon processing (Holst), the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov) and the biology of GLP-1 receptor signalling and degradation (Drucker) form one physiological discovery. It has been tested by large independent randomized trials and now extends from glycaemia to weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Maturity is not in question. On the chair's first question I define the achievement as the physiology and molecular identity of GLP-1, with the therapies named in the citation as the consequence and not as the thing honoured. I do not want a second part: no other shortlisted candidate matches B027 on mechanism and consequence, and a second part would force a reduction of the trio or a tenuous pairing. Citation: the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form, enabling incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity.
statement.case_against: The attribution risk is real and unresolved. The supplied material does not settle Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36)amide/(7-37) peptide against Habener and colleagues, who are outside the credit list. Knudsen's engineering of long-acting analogues is arguably what produced the clinical effect, so a physiology citation can read as honouring the hormone and not the medicine. If the committee cannot defend the Mojsov seat from the evidence in front of it, the choice between leaving a documented contributor out and shifting the citation toward therapy becomes a harder judgement than I have so far admitted. I have no evidence in the supplied record that would let me verify priority, and I will not pretend otherwise.

responses.point: The chair now supports Mojsov in the third seat after opening with Knudsen, and asks what evidence can settle Mojsov's priority against Habener and whether failure to settle it changes the Mojsov-or-Knudsen decision.
responses.response: I understand the chair's move and I share the discomfort he states, that his shift is not independent confirmation. In round 1 I said I would not oppose Knudsen if Mojsov's priority could not be substantiated, and I should sharpen that. The materials supplied contain no evidence that settles the Mojsov-Habener question. An unresolved priority question is a reason for care in the citation, but it is not enough to remove her. Her identification of the active truncated peptide is the molecular step that both the physiology and the later drug design rest on. Replacing her with Knudsen would change what the prize is for, from a discovery to a development, and I do not think the uncertainty alone justifies that. I keep Mojsov, with a citation that names the active form so that the claim is explicit and can be defended.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds that the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov set is the most defensible reading of the discovery itself, leaving drug engineering as translation, and that CAR-T and optogenetics have cleaner stories of impact or breadth but harder credit problems.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and it is the basis of my own position. On the second half I part from him on optogenetics. Breadth and originality are real, but six people have documented claims and the three-name cap forces an exclusion that I cannot justify from this material, which is why I keep it below B025. I also note that CAR-T is the cleaner fallback only on outcome. The Eshhar question remains, and June, Sadelain and Rosenberg describe different strands of work. If B027 were set aside I would still go to B025, but I would want the citation restricted to what those three can each be shown to have done.

responses.point: Sandberg warns that the committee may reward an exceptionally visible clinical story at the expense of older, cleaner mechanistic discoveries such as cGAS-STING and the unfolded protein response, and asks whether a two-part prize would be better.
responses.response: The warning is fair and I tested my own view against it. Visibility is not the reason I rank B027 first. The reason is that it has both a clear mechanism and independently verified outcomes. B020 and B043 have the clearer attribution, and Walter and Mori is as clean a pair as the list offers. But cGAS-STING has no therapeutic result yet, and for the UPR the link to human disease remains indirect, so I do not see them as ready to stand beside B027 this year. On a two-part prize, I would only support it if the second part were strong on its own, and I do not think any of them is. Pairing would also cost B027 one of its three names. I therefore stay with a single part, and I would revisit B043 or B020 in a later year.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that a single-achievement prize with a physiology-centred credit fits B027 better than a second part, which would dilute the strongest case, and ranks cGAS-STING above orexin as a second choice.
responses.response: I agree that a second part would dilute the strongest case, and I am glad that his argument rests on maturity that has appeared over decades and not on the prominence of semaglutide. I would add one thing from my own field. A prize for physiology should be able to show that the physiology is confirmed in patients, and B027 does. I agree with him about B020 as a second choice over B004, since the disease link for orexin depends on an autoimmune cause for human narcolepsy that has not been shown, and I know how hard it is to prove autoimmune etiology from association alone. I keep B025 ahead of B020 as my first fallback because B025 has a delivered clinical result, whereas B020 still has none.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be substantiated against Habener's group, which is not among the credited names. I cannot settle this from the supplied material.

Whether the committee would accept a physiology citation that leaves out the development of long-acting analogues (Knudsen), or whether a later reading of the prize as a drug prize would make the omission look wrong.
Whether B025 would need a different set of names than the supplied credit, given Eshhar's earlier chimeric-receptor work, if it became the fallback.
Whether the therapeutic status of B020 will change enough in the next few years to alter my ranking of it.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed since round 1. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My field is autoimmunity and rheumatology, so I am most familiar with B020 and B025 immunology, but this gives me no tie to any credited person. Co-authors Kuchroo and Sonesson are not on the shortlist, and a shared Karolinska setting does not establish a connection. I request no recusal.
